note: Non-blind check of the 10 empty-demand families whose members carry item-level examined demands, and of the 4 families assigned demands. Agent judgements from rendered pages.

families.author_reason_summary: Teaching derivations, assumption lists and numerical illustrations; they do not all require a complete identity proof, and the two members carrying item-level compound-angle demands cannot license the other sixteen.

members_checked.task: Activity 3.2 (pp.76-77, printed 62-63): 'Derive the rest of these formulae' - (i) cos(theta-phi) by replacing theta with 90-theta in sin(theta+phi) (tip given); (ii) cos(theta+phi) by replacing phi with -phi; (iii) tan(theta+phi) as sin/cos, tip says divide by cos theta cos phi; (iv) tan(theta-phi) by replacing phi with -phi.
members_checked.evidence: Each step is a tip-scripted substitution that rebuilds the standard expansions from sin(theta+phi); the exam parts for D02 (2023 P2 Q3(a) solve 2cos(theta+30)+5sin theta=4cos theta; 2024 P2 Q9(b) exact value of tan(x+3pi/4)) apply the expansions to a given expression or equation, which this activity never does.

members_checked.task: Discussion prompt after Activity 3.2: 'Are your results valid for all values of theta and phi?' and 'Test your results with theta=60, phi=30.'
members_checked.evidence: It is an unanswered self-check of the derived formulae (validity, and plugging in 60/30 where tan(90) is undefined), not an exact-evaluation or equation task; the 60/30 substitution is the closest point to 2024 P2 Q9(b)-style exact evaluation but has no target expression or posed answer.

families.notes: Both linked members sit on pp.76-77 inside the derivation of the compound-angle set; the worked example on p.77 (solve sin(theta+60)=cos(theta-60)) is the exam-like D02 task but is not a member here. Keeping the item-level D02 links visible while the family has no assessed demand is defensible. Context members were not opened.

families.author_reason_summary: Members recover sinusoid parameters from point values; only the worked example also covers range and exact values, and the two Try Now members do not assess those demands uniformly.

members_checked.task: f(x)=a+b cos x on 0<=x<=2pi with f(0)=10, f(2pi/3)=1: (a) find a and b (uses cos(2pi/3)=-cos(pi/3)=-1/2 via related angle), (b) state the range of f (-2<=y<=10), (c) exact value of f(5pi/6)=4-3sqrt3 (uses cos(5pi/6)=-sqrt3/2).
examined_demands: 8227:2020:M1:T6:O03:D01 Evaluate exact special-angle ratios and related angles
members_checked.evidence: Part (b) is the same one-line 'find the range of f' task as 2025 P1 Q7(c), and parts (a) and (c) require exact related-angle values (cos 2pi/3, cos 5pi/6) exactly as the syllabus D01 quote 'cos 150 = -sqrt3/2' describes; this is an exam-style posed example, not a derivation.

families.notes: The author is right that the range demand (T3:O02:D02) is not uniform: only Example 58 asks for a range. The author is wrong about exact values. Both context members also need exact special-angle values to set up their simultaneous equations: Try Now 58.1 uses cos(pi/3)=1/2 and cos(pi)=-1, and its hint explicitly reasons 'f(pi/3) is in the first quadrant, so +cos(pi/3)'; Try Now 58.2 uses sin(pi/6)=1/2 and sin(pi/2)=1. So M1:T6:O03:D01 is practised by all three members and can be set as the family demand and compared, for example with 2022 P1 Q9(b) and 2022 P2 Q3(a). The shared 'find a, b in a+b cos x / a+b sin x' response may also fit M1:T6:O02:D02 'Interpret transformed trig graph', whose exam parts are 2022 P1 Q10 and 2024 P1 Q9 ('two trig graphs parameters'); the author should consider it. Try Now members were seen on the same rendered page (p.226).

families.author_reason_summary: The proofs and explanations establish derivative rules instead of carrying out the syllabus differentiation calculation; the quotient-rule activity's single link does not extend to the other conceptual members.

members_checked.task: Activity 4.1 (printed p.87): 'Verify that the quotient rule gives dy/dx correctly when u=x^10 and v=x^7.' The learner applies the quotient rule to x^10/x^7 and checks the result, 3x^2, against differentiating x^3 directly.
members_checked.evidence: The quotient-rule formula is carried out, but on a degenerate monomial quotient that collapses to x^3 and only to confirm the rule; the exam parts (2024 P2 Q1: gradient of y=(2x-3)/(x-2) at x=-4; 2023 P2 Q5(a)) differentiate a genuine quotient, which is what Exercise 4A Q1 on the same page practises, not this activity.

families.notes: There is a wording defect in the author's reason: it says 'the quotient-rule activity's connected product-rule link', but the item-level demand recorded for Activity 4.1 is M2:T4:O02:D02 'Use quotient rule', not the product-rule demand D01. The author should correct the reason text. The member could fairly keep its item-level quotient-rule link, because it does execute the formula once, but it does not justify a family-level demand across the eight proof and explanation members, which were not opened.

families.author_reason_summary: The two posed examples ask for coordinate tables, a plotted curve and an explanation of a limit (one curve has a loop and is not a single explicit function). Their shared response is neither implicit nor parametric differentiation, and one item's explicit-function sketch tag cannot cover both.

members_checked.task: Example 4.19 (printed p.110): x=2t, y=36/t^2. (i) coordinates for t=+-1,+-2,+-3; (ii) plot the points and join them to give the curve; (iii) explain what happens as t->0 (y-axis is an asymptote).
members_checked.evidence: The task is to plot six tabulated parametric points and join them, with no function notation, no specified domain and no inverse. The exam parts for this demand (2022 P1 Q6(c): sketch f(x)=ln(x-2) and its inverse on one diagram, showing axis intersections; 2021 P1 Q12(c)) ask for a function-and-inverse sketch, which this example does not practise.

families.notes: The context member, Example 4.20 (p.125: x=t^2, y=t^3-t, table, sketch, 'values of x for which the curve is undefined'), has a loop and is not an explicit function, as the author says. Parametric curve plotting by table is not one of the listed 8227 demands; the only parametric demand is the derivative (M2:T4:O03). Keeping the item-level sketch link on Example 4.19 is generous but harmless; it is not a reason to compare the family.

families.author_reason_summary: The selected comparison combines partial fractions with a negative-index series expansion that lies outside the 8227 binomial scope; the combined method cannot be treated as an ordinary elementary-integral demand.

members_checked.task: Exercise 8E Q3 (printed p.202, PS): (i)(a) express 3/((1+x)(1-2x)) in partial fractions; (i)(b) hence find the integral from 0 to 0.1 to 5 d.p.; (ii)(a) first three terms of 3(1+x)^-1(1-2x)^-1; (ii)(b) use them to approximate the same integral; (ii)(c) percentage error.
members_checked.evidence: Only (i)(b) is exam-like: integrating 1/(1+x)+2/(1-2x) from 0 to 0.1 is the same reciprocal-linear definite integral as 2021 P2 Q2 (prove the integral from 1 to 4 of 8/(2x+1) is ln 81). But it is reachable only through the partial-fraction step (i)(a), and (ii)(a)-(c) need a negative-index binomial series that the 8227 limit QUAL02 excludes, so the item as posed is not a fair 8227 comparison item.

families.notes: The author's reason is incomplete: it names only the negative-index series as out of scope, but partial fractions (i)(a) also has no 8227 demand. No 'partial fraction' text appears in the demand registry or the curriculum files. The reason should say both prerequisites are outside 8227. If the author ever wants a comparable item, the in-scope core is (i)(b) with the decomposition supplied; as written, comparing the whole item would overstate the match.

families.author_reason_summary: The illustrations derive logarithm properties from an area definition; the one activity that estimates e does not make every member a numerical-e evaluation task.

members_checked.task: Activity 2.7 (printed p.47): with a calculator area-finding facility or other technology, use the fact that the integral from 1 to e of 1/x dx = 1 to find e to 2 d.p., knowing it lies between 2 and 3.
examined_demands: 8227:2020:M2:T2:O02:D01 Use exponential and natural log definitions
members_checked.evidence: The activity is a technology-dependent numerical search for the upper limit of an area, built on the textbook's L(x) area definition of ln x. The only exam part for this demand (2022 P1 Q6(b): find the inverse of f(x)=ln(x-2)) uses ln and e^x as inverse functions, which this activity does not practise.

families.notes: Defining ln x as an area is not the 8227 route; the syllabus treats e^x and ln x as inverse functions with their graphs, and integrating 1/x appears only through reverse differentiation. The four context members (Activities 2.4-2.6 and Prompt 3: product-law derivations, the power-rule exception) are the same teaching scaffold and were not opened.

families.author_reason_summary: The contexts mix musical ratios, cell growth, earthquakes and decibels, with different series and exponential responses and defects. No one examined demand is assessed by every member; the item-level links stay visible.

members_checked.task: Chapter-opening prompt (printed p.24): a cell divides into two every 24 hours, starting from one cell. How many cells after (i) 5 days and (ii) 10 days? Approximately how many days to reach one million cells? (32; 1024; 20)
examined_demands: 8227:2020:M1:T2:O03:D02 Solve GP terms and finite sums
members_checked.evidence: Finding the first n with 2^n >= 10^6 in a growth context has the same structure as 2024 P1 Q4(b) ('in which operation does the pump first extract less than 10 cm^3?'), and the 5- and 10-day counts are GP terms. The caveat: it is an opener prompt that asks for an 'approximately' answer and the text expects trial powers of 2 rather than logarithms.

members_checked.task: Exercise 2A Q6 (printed p.28, M): octave frequencies double. (i) frequency of B three octaves above middle (247x2^3=1976); (ii) which note is 27.5 Hz and how many octaves below the middle (A, three); (iii) how many standard-scale notes lie in 75-9000 Hz.
examined_demands: 8227:2020:M1:T2:O03:D02 Solve GP terms and finite sums
members_checked.evidence: The posed parts find GP terms with r=2 for a given number of steps, (ii) solves 220/2^n=27.5 for n, and (iii) bounds GP terms between 75 and 9000 for each note letter. That is the nth-term-in-context work of 2024 P1 Q4(a)/(b), at a lower level: the numbers allow plain doubling and no sums are needed.

members_checked.task: Exercise 2B Q13 (printed p.35, M): Richter strength = log10(E/63000). (i) strength for E=2.5x10^11 J; (ii) energy for strength 7.4; (iii) how many times more energy in a 7.1 quake than a 4.2 quake (10^2.9, about 794).
members_checked.evidence: Parts (ii) and (iii) solve a given logarithmic model for the unknown quantity by moving between log and exponential form. This is the same model-inversion task as 2021 P2 Q4(b) (N=5000e^(-0.02t): number of full weeks before N halves), although (i) is only an evaluation.

members_checked.task: Exercise 2B Q14 (printed p.36, M): decibels. (i) solve x^10=10; (ii) show B (36 dB) is 26% louder than A (35 dB); (iii) how many dB increase doubles loudness (solve 1.259^n=2, n about 3); (iv) explain Amir's percentage mistake.
members_checked.evidence: Part (iii) is exactly 'use logarithms to solve a^x=b' in context (n = log 2 / log 10^0.1), which is the 2021 P2 Q4(b) halving-time demand. Parts (i) and (ii) are its set-up, and only (iv) is a different explanation task.

families.notes: The author's reason is literally true: no one demand covers all six members. The context members are Activity 2.2 (p.43: unposed 'relationships' on log scales) and Example 2.6 (p.51: fitting a straight line to raw temperature data), and neither practises these demands. But four of the six members are posed, answered, exam-style practice of examined demands in two coherent sub-groups. (1) GP growth/doubling context: Prompt 1 and Exercise 2A Q6, for M1:T2:O03:D02/D03, comparable with 2024 P1 Q4(a)/(b) and 2021 P1 Q8. (2) Solve a log/exponential model for the unknown: Exercise 2B Q13 and Q14, for M2:T2:O03:D01, comparable with 2021 P2 Q4(b). The right remedy is to split the family and compare each sub-group, not to leave everything uncompared because the mixed family has no common demand.

families.author_reason_summary: The examples expose the limits of sign searches and of even-multiplicity roots, and one is an unposed illustration; one item's explicit bracket/graph demand does not make every selected response an executed bracket method.

members_checked.task: Exercise 6A Q8 (printed p.151, PS): for y=1/x, y=x/(x^2+1) and y=x^2/(x^2+1), (a) sketch the curve, (b) write down any roots, (c) investigate what happens with a change-of-sign method on the starting interval [-0.3, 0.7].
members_checked.evidence: Only (ii)(c) is an ordinary sign-change bracket of a continuous function, as in 2025 P2 Q12(c) ('show by calculation that the smaller root lies between 1.68 and 1.71'). (i)(c) is a false sign change across the pole at 0 and (iii)(c) is a touching root with no sign change, and these failure analyses are the point of the question; no exam part asks for them. The sketches are standalone curves read for an obvious root, not the function-and-inverse sketch of T3:O05:D01 or the two-graph intersection count of 2025 P2 Q12(a).

families.notes: The other member (Worked-illustration 3, p.163: touching root, clustered roots, discontinuity) is an unposed illustration. The item-level links on Q8 overstate it slightly. T3:O05:D01 'sketch graphs of functions and their inverses for a specified domain' does not really fit sketching y=1/x and similar curves, and the author could drop that link. Partial overlap remains in (ii)(c) and in the (a)/(b) sketch-then-roots pattern, but those are not the item's distinctive response.

families.author_reason_summary: The selected prompts discuss certainty, trials or stopping assumptions; one prompt's connected bracket/stopping tag is not an executed numerical-root procedure in every member.

members_checked.task: Prompt (printed p.155, CP): after the text supplies the iterates 1, 0.8, 0.6655, 0.6261, 0.6192 and the values f(0.61)=+0.034 and f(0.62)=-0.0083, 'Explain why you are certain that your judgement is now correct.'
members_checked.evidence: The bracket values are supplied, so the learner only states the conclusion (a sign change of a continuous f means a root lies in [0.61, 0.62]). Exam parts such as 2025 P2 Q12(c) ('show by calculation that the smaller root lies between 1.68 and 1.71') and 2021 P2 Q8(a) require the evaluation as well, and no iteration or stopping rule is carried out here.

families.notes: The prompt does cover the concluding statement that the exam's sign-change mark needs, so the item-level D02 link is reasonable. The O04:D02 stopping/precision link is weak: the prompt does not ask for a root to a stated accuracy, and the [0.61, 0.62] bracket does not even settle the 2 d.p. value. The context members (Prompt 1, Prompt 6, Activity 6.1) are discussion and error-model prompts and were not opened.

families.author_reason_summary: The vector proof prompts mix assumptions, general claims and an internal-ratio theorem proof; the one connected geometric item cannot license a shared direct vector-calculation demand across all six members.

members_checked.task: CP prompt after Example 10.8 (printed p.247): 'The above example made use of the ratio theorem. Prove that when C divides AB in the ratio s:t then OC = t/(s+t) a + s/(s+t) b.'
members_checked.evidence: It is an unanswered general symbolic proof in s and t. The exam parts (2023 P1 Q7(a)(ii): find OC given numeric OA, OB and AB=BC; 2022 P1 Q11(a): show OR=(-1,5,4) in a trapezium with RQ=2OP) apply the same OC=OA+lambda*AB reasoning to specific numeric vectors, which is what Example 10.8 just above does, not this prompt.

families.notes: The route (position vector = OA + fraction of AB) is identical to the exam's, so the item-level links are fair, but the general-ratio proof form is not how 8227 asks it. The exam-like item is Example 10.8 (C divides AB in the ratio 2:3), which is not a member of this family. The other five members (assumptions, a 3-D length claim, a commutativity proof, a 3-D angle proof) were not opened.

families.author_reason_summary: Both sources explicitly ask for the coordinates where d2y/dx2=0 on y=x e^(-x/2). That uses second-derivative notation and computation directly; no stationary-point test is claimed. Assigned: M1:T8:O01:D02 'Use first and second derivative notation'.

members_checked.task: Exercise 4B Q10 (printed p.95; Cambridge 9709/2 Q6 Nov 2008): find the exact coordinates of the point on y = x e^(-x/2) at which d2y/dx2 = 0. Answer (4, 4e^-2).
examined_demands: assigned: 8227:2020:M1:T8:O01:D02 Use first and second derivative notation
members_checked.evidence: The item does compute and use d2y/dx2 (D02 holds), but the work that earns the marks is the product rule on x times e^(-x/2), applied twice, with the chain rule on the exponential. That is the 2022 P2 Q5(a) task (y=6x e^(x/3): gradient condition) almost exactly, and the assignment omits it.

members_checked.task: Try Now 42 Q2 (printed p.514): find the exact coordinates of the point on y = x e^(-x/2) at which d2y/dx2 = 0 (the same question as Goldie 4B Q10).
examined_demands: assigned: 8227:2020:M1:T8:O01:D02 Use first and second derivative notation
item-level: 8227:2020:M2:T4:O01:D01 Differentiate exponential log and trig functions
members_checked.evidence: It is the identical function and request, so it needs the same product rule and exponential chain-rule work. Its item-level tags leave out the product rule (M2:T4:O02:D01) that the Goldie copy carries, an inconsistency between two copies of one question.

families.notes: D02 is a valid family demand, but its only example part (2023 P1 Q11: f(x)=9/sqrt(3-2x), find f' and f'') needs the chain rule on a power, not product or exponential differentiation, so the comparison under-represents what these members practise. Both members uniformly require M2:T4:O02:D01 (product rule) and M2:T4:O01:D02 (composite exponential), and 2022 P2 Q5(a) is a near-identical exam match. Recommend adding both demands at family level and aligning the YM member's item-level tags with the Goldie copy. The author is right not to claim a stationary-point test, since d2y/dx2=0 here is a point of inflection and is not classified.

families.author_reason_summary: Both source groups explicitly ask for differentiation with y depending on x, keeping dy/dx and the product/chain terms. The author calls this an assessed implicit-differentiation building block, not full curve work, and labels it 'directly assessed (limited response)'. Assigned: M2:T4:O03:D01 'Differentiate implicit curve'.

members_checked.task: Example 4.15 (printed p.102): differentiate with respect to x (i) y^2, (ii) xy, (iii) 3x^2y^3, (iv) sin y; the worked solution uses the chain rule with dy/dx and the product rule.
members_checked.evidence: The members carry out the term-by-term step of implicit differentiation, for example d/dx(3x^2y^3) = 3xy^2(3x dy/dx + 2y), the same move as differentiating y^3 sin 2x in 2023 P2 Q8(a). But there is no curve equation, dy/dx is never isolated and nothing is 'used', so only part of 'find and use the first derivative of a function defined implicitly' is assessed.

members_checked.task: Exercise 4D Q1 (printed p.106): differentiate with respect to x (i) y^4, (ii) x^2+y^3-5, (iii) xy+x+y, (iv) cos y, (v) e^(y+2), (vi) xy^3, (vii) 2x^2y^5, (viii) x+ln y-3, (ix) x e^y - cos y, (x) x^2 ln y, (xi) x e^(sin y), (xii) x tan y - y tan x.
members_checked.evidence: All twelve parts are the same expression-level step, mixing chain rule on y with the product rule, as in the textbook's worked example. None forms a curve equation and solves for dy/dx, which the exam parts require (2023 P2 Q8(a): from y^3 sin 2x + 4y = 8, show dy/dx = -2y^3 cos 2x/(3y^2 sin 2x + 4)).

families.notes: The assignment is defensible, and the author's 'limited response' label already admits the gap. The comparison output should state that these members practise the differentiation step only, not isolating dy/dx or using it for a gradient or tangent. Both members also contain product-rule sub-parts (xy, 3x^2y^3, xy^3, 2x^2y^5, x e^y, x^2 ln y, x e^(sin y), x tan y), and the exam implicit parts 2023 P2 Q8(a) and 2025 P2 Q5 also carry M2:T4:O02:D01 (product rule). The author could consider adding it, but not every sub-part uses it.

families.author_reason_summary: The source explicitly asks for the x values where ln(3x) and ln(x) share the stated gradient/shape relationship, so the learner must determine x>0. Assigned: M1:T3:O02:D01 'Determine admissible domain'.

members_checked.task: Discussion prompt after Example 4.8 (printed p.92): 'The gradient function found in part (ii) above for y=ln(3x) is the same as that for y=ln x. What does this tell you about the shapes of the two curves? For what values of x is it valid?'
examined_demands: item-level only: 8227:2020:M2:T2:O02:D02 Interpret inverse relation and graphs
members_checked.evidence: The 'for what values of x is it valid?' sub-part requires stating the common domain x>0 of ln(3x) and ln x. That is the same one-mark domain recognition as 2022 P1 Q6(a) (smallest k for f(x)=ln(x-2), x>k), so the assigned demand is genuinely, if minimally, assessed.

families.notes: There is a consistency caveat. This is an unposed '?' discussion prompt with no printed answer, yet here it is treated as directly assessed, while similar unposed prompts elsewhere stay supporting-only (for example Goldie C3 Prompt 3, 'test your results with theta=60, phi=30'). The author should apply one rule to unposed prompts. The prompt's main question, about shape (y=ln 3x is y=ln x translated up by ln 3), is left uncompared. That is reasonable, because no exam part asks for that translation reading; the exam's ln-graph parts are sketches of a function and its inverse.

families.author_reason_summary: The posed parts calculate separation and speeds as vector magnitudes, then use the same time in two position vectors to decide whether the boats collide; the given linear position models need no formal line-equation derivation. Assigned: M1:T7:O04:D01 'Calculate magnitude' and M1:T7:O02:D03 'Interpret geometric vector relation'.

members_checked.task: Exercise 10E Q3 (printed p.270, PS): cargo vessel r1=12t i+16t j, fishing boat r2=(10-3t)i+(8+4t)j (km, hours). (i) How far apart are they when the cargo vessel leaves harbour? (ii) How fast is each boat travelling? (iii) What happens to the boats?
members_checked.evidence: (i) needs |r2(0)-r1(0)| = |10i+8j| = sqrt164, about 12.8 km, and (ii) needs |12i+16j| = 20 and |-3i+4j| = 5: magnitude calculations of the kind in 2023 P1 Q7(b)(i). (i) and (iii) also need the difference of two position vectors read as a separation, and equal position vectors at the same t (t=2/3, the point (8, 32/3)) read as the same point. That is the geometric reading of vector subtraction and equality that 2023 P1 Q7(a)(ii) and 2022 P1 Q11(a) use.

families.notes: D03 fits less tightly than D01. The collision step is closer to 'use position vectors' (M1:T7:O03:D03), which the author could add or substitute. A minor data point: the author's stored derived answer for (i) is '64/5', the 3 s.f. key value 12.8, while the exact separation is sqrt164 = 2sqrt41, about 12.806 km. The method text says this correctly, but the stored value should not be read as exact.
